Radical cure is inappropriate for patients living within an endemic area since re-infection is likely and therefore WHO3 recom- mends that it should be limited to patients resident in areas where transmission is very low or absent, and it may be attempted during an epidemic; other patients should sim- ply be treated with a further course of chloroquine in the event of relapse or re-infection. Severe vivax malaria should be treated the same way as severe and complicated falciparum malaria (see above).3 Treatment of malaria during pregnancy. Malaria is es- pecially dangerous during pregnancy and the seriousness of the disease usually outweighs any potential risk from treatment. Malaria infection during pregnancy can result in maternal anaemia, hypoglycaemia, pulmonary oedema, miscarriage, premature birth, congenital malaria infection, low birth-weight, and neonatal death.10,12 Pregnant women living in areas where malaria transmission is low or unstable have little or no acquired immunity and are 2 to 3 times more likely to develop severe disease than non- pregnant women living in the same area;3,10 however, those living in endemic areas where malaria transmission is high have often acquired partial immunity. For pregnant women living in endemic areas quinine plus follow-on treatment with clindamycin may be given for treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria in the first trimester. Data regarding the use of artemisinin derivatives in the first trimester is at present limited; however, ACTs may be given if no other effective treatment is available. In the second or third trimester ACTs, artesunate, or quinine may be given, plus follow-on treatment with clindamy- cin.3 For the treatment of severe malaria in the first trimes- ter quinine or artesunate may be used;2,3 however, care should be taken that patients given quinine do not become hypoglycaemic. Artemisinin derivatives (particularly artesunate) are the drugs of choice for treatment of severe malaria in the second and third trimesters.2,3 In non-endemic areas it is recommended that falciparum malaria in pregnancy be treated with quinine plus follow- on treatment with clindamycin.8-10 Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) or mefloquine may be given as alternatives where first-line treatment is not tolerated or no other treat- ment options are available.10 Although fetal abnormalities have been associated with the use of high doses of chloro- quine, extensive clinical experience suggests it is safe; its value is limited, however, due to resistance.
